entries.title: Can PM Modi reconnect with India's Gen Z?
entries.summary: Student protests exposed a growing disconnect between PM Narendra Modi's BJP and young Indians. Experts say Instagram reels alone won't close it.
entries.content:
India

Can PM Modi reconnect with India's Gen Z?

August 3, 2026

Student protests exposed a growing disconnect between PM Narendra Modi's BJP and young Indians. Experts say Instagram reels alone won't close it.

As students filled India's streets to demand accountability from the government, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi seemed to have realized that he needed to connect more effectively with the country's youth.

Modi posted on Instagram a rare selfie video in which he said he was pained by their suffering and promised remedial steps. But it was not enough to satisfy the protesters' concerns, and five Gen Z-style reels later, that gap seems as wide as ever.

"We ain't friends," one comment under the first reel read. It echoed thousands of others reacting to a midnight video drop from the PM.

In one of Modi's lesser-produced videos, he addressed the youth as "friends" before finally speaking about the exam at the center of the protests.

It was the prime minister’s response to the biggest political crisis he has faced in his third term so far, over a cancelled high-stakes medical entrance exam which affected millions of aspirants.

Since the first video, he's improved camera angles and lighting, tried varied backgrounds, and even started and ended the videos himself like a one-man content creator. The response remains tepid.

For Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the protests came at the peak of its power, but the unrest has dimmed that shine, and the disconnect with the youth is substantial, experts told DW.

Young voices sidelined

In 2024, the average age of MPs elected to India's Parliament reached a record 56 years, which is a problem, said Shipra Baduni, CEO of Young Leaders for Active Citizenship, because there is not much youth representation in the legislature.

The second shift is in the nation's youth politics.

India has traditionally had vibrant youth participation at the university level, where student parties have long been affiliated with national and regional parties. 

"Student politics has not only given a pulse check, or given a platform for young people to be able to express frustration, or anger, or dissent," said Baduni. "It's also given some of these parties and leaders today."

"We've seen systematically over the last one decade that it has been cut down," she added. "There is a very evident push to say that students should only study, and there is no need for students to engage in politics."

"Where is the space for a young person to express their frustration? If you go on social media to criticize the government, there is a crackdown. Offices are screening your social media."

But Baduni believes the responsibility to connect with the youth doesn't lie with the central government alone: "It's the job of my ward councillor or my local elected leader to come out and say, 'let me talk to the young people in my locality, what are your concerns?'."

DW reached out to BJP's youth leader for New Delhi and the party's national spokesperson, but did not receive a response from either.

Decoding the Gen Z vibe

Memes and music formed the backbone of reels posted on social media, while some young adults politely made their demands and others used expletives in sing-song slogans.

When the government responded, that response itself became fodder for a new wave of memes and content.

"The BJP does not understand expression of anger through ironic humor/memes, because their strategy was focused on the WhatsApp generation," political scientist and author Amit Julka told DW.

"Even now, let's say the BJP's PR department were to say we are now going to crack the Gen Z code, the result will be fundamentally inorganic."

Over a week after the protests were called off following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the national conversation has shifted — not to education reform and preventing paper leaks, but to "misguided youths."

Several BJP members and supporters posted messages saying the abuses were against Indian moral codes and had deeply unsettled them. They were referring to a viral video where a teenage girl used abusive language against the Prime Minister and his late mother.

In a reel posted over the weekend, Modi addressed the teenager's words.

"I can fully understand the outrage within society. It comes as a cultural shock to see our daughters using such language," Modi said, adding that he wanted to "forgive them" rather than see them dragged through court proceedings.

Modi's senior ministerial colleague Rajnath Singh said last weekend that the government's "top priority remains to understand our students' genuine concerns, ​address them promptly, and ensure that they know their voices are being heard."

Julka pointed to this episode as one way the BJP can delegitimize dissenters going forward. "There doesn't necessarily need to be an application of coercion. Sometimes even a veiled allusion is enough," he said, adding that Gen Zs were ultimately "vulnerable" youth.

What can bridge the political gap?

Working at the cross-section of youth and policy, Baduni believes the BJP still has non-coercive ways to bridge the gap. First, by staying on topic.

"The agenda of the protest is the systematic failure of the education system in India that has failed so many people. Why are you, even today, not talking about that?" she asked.

Baduni suggested that the BJP government needs to speak with the youth at various civic levels and make constructive changes while refraining from further crackdowns.

"I'm not sure how much of it is going to reverse the dent that has already been made," she said, adding that it could give the BJP a better sense of the issues that matter to young people and help the party begin addressing them.

"If you tell them that they will only be heard if they're disruptive, then there is no incentive for them to not be disruptive," Baduni noted.

Since the protests against the education minister ended, several smaller demonstrations have been reported across India.

In Uttar Pradesh's Fatehpur, hundreds of students staged a peaceful walkout to bring the district's attention to infrastructure gaps. In a government school in western India, students protested to demand more teachers. In Jaipur, three student leaders began an indefinite hunger strike, demanding restoration of student union elections.

As for Modi's series of reels, both Baduni and Julka said the one-sided interaction wasn't a real solution.

"That will just give Gen Z a lot more content on what's wrong with this government," said Baduni.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Indian court acquits ex-wrestling chief of harassment
entries.summary: While the court ruled in lawmaker Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh's favor, female athletes say their legal battle is not over. The case sparked months of protests by India's leading female wrestlers.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

While the court ruled in lawmaker Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh's favor, female athletes say their legal battle is not over. The case sparked months of protests by India's leading female wrestlers.

An Indian court on Monday acquitted the former head of the country's wrestling federation of sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by female athletes.

Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh, a former lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had denied allegations that he groped wrestlers and demanded sexual favors.

What was the reaction to Singh's acquittal?

Singh's lawyer Rajiv Mohan said the New Delhi court found "inconsistencies" in witness statements and "contradictions on major issues."

"I had complete faith that justice would be done," Singh told reporters after the verdict. "I never considered myself a criminal at all."

Supporters celebrated outside the court by setting off firecrackers, showering Singh with flower petals and offering him sweets.

Leading female wrestler Vinesh Phogat said the women would challenge the ruling in a higher court and continue their legal fight.

"It took a great deal of courage for us to take to the streets and get a complaint registered against a powerful leader of the ruling party," she wrote on X.

What is the significance of the case?

The allegations triggered months of protests in New Delhi in 2023, led by prominent athletes including Phogat, Olympic bronze medalist Sakshi Malik and Olympic medalist Bajrang Punia.

Hundreds joined sit-in demonstrations accusing authorities of failing to act against Singh.

Malik later retired from wrestling in protest, while Punia returned one of India's highest civilian honors.

Delhi police charged Singh in 2023 after sustained pressure from the protesting wrestlers.

A court formally brought charges against him in 2024 over allegations involving five women.

Singh completed his parliamentary term that year and was not selected to run again. The BJP instead fielded his son from the same constituency, which he won.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?
entries.summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

What happens next for Infantino and FIFA?

August 3, 2026

FIFA President Gianni Infantino is under pressure after the failure of his plan to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup. But will he be ousted? And what is needed for that to happen?

Now that Gianno Infantino has shelved his plans to create a commercial subsidiary for the World Cup and other FIFA events, UEFA's boycott of FIFA events is over and matches now appear less in danger. Nevertheless, the European governing body says it is now "rebuilding trust" with FIFA — and the story continues to develop rapidly.

As a result, increased focus will be put on women's football when the U20 World Cup starts on September 5 in Poland, and when the U17 World Cup starts in October in Morocco. There are also matches around the world that will decide the qualifiers for next summer's World Cup in Brazil in the same month. Despite there being scant mention in FIFA's subsidiary proposal of the women's game, it will be the first test of life after it.

While a boycott is now off the table, the games will be harder to navigate given the current chaos around the sport's governing body. This is far from ideal for the teams competing, particularly given the tournament's importance.

Football associations have pull support for Infantino

With UEFA, Europe's football governors, forming a united front, it is assumed that most, if not all, football associations on the continent will withdraw their support in the coming days.

The first nation to publicly drop their support for Gianni Infantino was Finland, last week. Wales followed on Monday, saying in a statement that "failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept," before England followed suit later in the day.

Germany's FA (DFB) is the biggest sports association in the world, but has yet to officially withdraw its support. It is expected to though, especially when considering the recent words of DFB Director Andreas Rettig. The 63-year-old recently told Stern magazine in an interview that Infantino's recent actions have led to "an irreparable loss of trust" and that football needs to "hit the reset button. We need a different culture. Because trust is the hardest currency."

"From my perspective, Mr. Infantino has invested a great deal of time, money, and energy into maintaining his power structure. Clearly, many decisions served primarily to consolidate his own position," added Retting.

FIFA presidential election next year

The election for Infantino's post is on March 18, 2027, at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, Morocco.

He will run for re-election as president for a final four-year term, looking to gain 106 votes from FIFA's 211 member states (Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10) to win. Each state gets a vote and voting is done in a secret ballot, which takes time.

However, it seems as though Infantino is increasingly under pressure, and if 19 of the 37 members of the FIFA Council, the organization's main executive body, call for an emergency meeting in the next two weeks, he could be asked to resign. Several members of the council, including Germany's Bernd Neuendorf, have publicly crititcized Infantino for failing to consult them about his latest plans.

There might also be an Extraordinary FIFA Congress if 43 associations formally request it. Given that UEFA has 55 members, it holds the power to request it at any time. For Infantino to be voted out through a vote of no confidence, 106 votes would be required.

Before his venture to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors ended in chaos after widespread condemnation, Infantino looked almost certain to win re-election. The reported revenues from this summer's World Cup were $15 billion (€13 billion), a significantly higher number than expected and one that would have strengthened his position in the organization, given that much of it would be redistibuted among the member organizations.

No clear candidates to succeed Infantino

There has been a lot of speculation about who might succeed Infantino since his position has come under threat in the last week, but it is too soon to really know the legitimacy of any claims. In any case, any potential challengers must declare their candidacy by 18 November.

Nasser Al-Khelaifi, the Paris Saint-Germain chairman, had been touted as a potential candidate given his increasingly influential position in world football. However, the Qatari recently ruled himself out, with a representative for the executive reportedly saying via Politico: "Nasser has absolutely no ambition, no intention, no interest in the Fifa role." Qatar is one of the few federations to have publicly backed Infantino in recent days.

The most obvious candidate is the current UEFA President, Alexander Ceferin, but the Slovenian lawyer is reportedly also not interested in the role.

Concacaf (the confederation of North and Central America and the Caribbean) president Victor Montagliani is one of the few candidates who has expressed interest in the role in the past, but it is unclear whether the man who speaks English, French, Italian and Spanish is ready to challenge now.

Outspoken Norwegian FA President Lise Klaveness has supporters, and, after an initial failure, reached the UEFA Executive Committee in 2025. But the outspoken style that has won her admirers is thought not to have the broad appeal needed in a FIFA candidate. Some also believe her gender may count against her.

Finally, AFC chief, Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who lost out to Infantino in the 2016 election, could be a contender if the AFC breaks ranks from FIFA in the way UEFA have. A member of Bahrain’s ruling House of Khalifa, the 60-year-old called Infantino's actions "totally unacceptable" and may be tempted to go against him again, though human rights questions contributed to his previous defeat.

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: Russia: Bridge-building with North Korea
entries.summary: In the far east, well away from world events, Russia and North Korea are building their first road connection. The project has set alarm bells ringing in Ukraine.
entries.content:
North Korea

Unraveling Russia's bridge project with North Korea

August 3, 2026

In the far east, well away from world events, Russia and North Korea are building their first road connection. The project has set alarm bells ringing in Ukraine.

For years, Khasan was little more than a very remote place on the edge of Russia. Less than 500 people live in the village in the country's far east, more than 5,600 miles (9,012 kilometers) from Moscow. But it's here that Russia shares a mere 10.5-mile border with North Korea — and Khasan is the only Russian settlement along that short stretch. Since 1959, the so-called Korean-Russian Friendship Railway Bridge has crossed the Tumen River here, serving as the only land connection between the two countries.

But in recent years, Russia and North Korea have been building a parallel road bridge just a few hundred yards away. The bridge is now nearing completion ahead of schedule, raising concerns in Kyiv that Russia could use it to secretly bring North Korean troops to the front lines in Ukraine.

Since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow and Pyongyang haveimproved their ties. Both countries face Western sanctions and are diplomatically largely isolated. In June 2024, Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership deal which in part focused on expanding military cooperation. That meant large-scale weapons shipments as well as the deployment of North Korean soldiers to support Russia's war in Ukraine. At the same time, both governments agreed to build the new road bridge.

"The opening of the new bridge will boost bilateral trade, optimize logistics, strengthen cultural ties and transform border regions into dynamically growing economic centers," Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said at the time.

The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has also pointed to the bridge's economic significance, noting that "the pace at which construction of the road bridge is progressing, and the continued high level of rail traffic at previously dormant rail yards, are clear indicators of the importance and expansion of trade between the two countries during Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine."

A project for trade and tourism?

But according to British newspaper The Guardian, there are major doubts that civilian economic goals are the project's true primary purpose.

Official data shows that trade between Russia and North Korea amounted to just $34 million in 2024. The bridge and its immediate infrastructure are thought to cost roughly $100 million. Satellite pictures of the site show warehouses, customs facilities, truck areas and a helicopter pad being built.

Ukrainian human rights organization Truth Hounds, which has been monitoring the project, also doubts the bridge is for tourism. It is about 125 hours by car from Moscow and about four hours from Vladivostok.

"Tourism in North Korea is heavily restricted and, given the country's isolation, cannot expand rapidly," the organization said. If anyone from Russia would visit North Korea, they probably would go to the capital, Pyongyang, rather than the country's remote northeastern region. But Pyongyang is hundreds of miles from the border, and "few people would want to make that journey by car," the group argued.

Russia has spent years trying to get tourists to take heavily subsidized flights to visit Pyongyang. However, not many have taken up the opportunity. In 2025, fewer than 10,000 Russian citizens are thought to have traveled to North Korea.

Or a cover for military transport?

Truth Hounds instead concludes that the bridge's real purpose is to deepen military cooperation, particularly by facilitating the transfer of North Korean troops and weapons for the war in Ukraine.

According to unofficial information reported by South Korean, Ukrainian and US sources in the middle of last year, North Korea sent between 14,000 and 15,000 personnel to support Russia's war, with many reportedly deployed in Russia's Kursk region while parts of it were under Ukrainian control. North Korea has also supplied Russia with weapons.

Road transport, Truth Hounds suggests, is harder to monitor by satellite than rail transport. Trains are confined to fixed tracks, and loading and unloading can take place only at designated rail hubs. Trucks however, can load and unload almost anywhere and satellite surveillance is virtually impossible.

Just days ago, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on X that Russia could deploy as many as 30,000 additional North Korean troops in the war against Ukraine.

Military know-how for North Korea

Zelenskyy also argued that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un from the improved military partnership. The new bridge could enable Russia to secretly move resources into North Korea.

"Russia," Zelenskyy wrote, "is helping North Korea learn how to wage modern war, improve its weapons and gain real combat experience in using them."

Observers also believe that North Korea might be receiving some Russian nuclear technology in exchange for helping Moscow in its war efforts.

Taken together, Zelenskyy warned in his X post, these developments pose "a threat to everyone in Asia who lives within range of North Korean missiles."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Germany news: Calls intensify to ban Meta Glasses
entries.summary: Both rights groups and regulators say the new AI tech is dangerous to consumers. At the same time, debate is heating up over pension reforms. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Calls intensify to ban Meta Glasses

Published August 3, 2026last updated August 3, 2026

Both rights groups and regulators say the new AI tech is dangerous to consumers. At the same time, debate is heating up over pension reforms. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • DAX breaks soards to new high on hopes of US-Iran talks
  • So-called "smart glasses" have ignited fierce controversy in privacy-conscious Germany
  • The Bundestag may reopen negotiations on pension reforms after criticism from some conservative leaders

Here are the latest headlines, reports and analyses from across Germany on Monday, August 3: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section Drought and disease hit German sugar beet harvest

Drought and disease hit German sugar beet harvest

Drought, extreme heat and disease are taking a heavy toll on sugar beet crops in Germany, with production in the south expected to fall by around a third from last year.

The Association of South German Sugar Beet Growers said such a yield would be the lowest since German reunification in 1990.

The poor harvest could also push up consumer prices, with crops suffering in France, Europe's largest sugar beet producer, as well.

Even fields in southern Germany that normally have reliable water supplies are showing clear signs of drought stress.

The association said weakened plants are more vulnerable to disease, causing some beets to develop a rubbery texture and reducing the amount of sugar that can be extracted.

The organization represents nearly 10,000 growers across seven regional associations. Its members cultivate around 100,000 hectares of sugar beet and supply seven factories.

Skip next section Germany calls Rhine low-water conference

Germany calls Rhine low-water conference

Germany's transport minister has called an expert conference in Bonn for Thursday as record-low water levels on the Rhine severely disrupt freight shipping.

A ministry spokesperson said Steffen Bilger had arranged the meeting at short notice, although the list of participants was still being drawn up.

The city of Cologne recorded its lowest Rhine level since measurements began on Saturday. Düsseldorf and Duisburg also reported historic lows over the weekend, sharply limiting how much cargo vessels can carry.

North Rhine-Westphalia Transport Minister Oliver Krischer has already called for a national task force bringing together the federal government, states, municipalities and the logistics industry.

Water levels have also fallen sharply along other major rivers, including the Elbe and Danube, with many monitoring stations recording new lows over the weekend.

Germany's Federal Institute of Hydrology said prolonged heat and dry weather were continuing to drain rivers across the country, while brief showers brought only temporary relief.

"Overall, the downward trend continues to dominate," the institute said.

Skip next section DAX breaks soards to new high on hopes of US-Iran talks

DAX breaks soards to new high on hopes of US-Iran talks

Germany's DAX index has climbed above 26,000 points for the first time as hopes of easing tensions between the United States and Iran lifted markets.

The benchmark passed its previous record of 25,900.10 points shortly after trading began on Monday and hovered around the 26,000 mark by midday.

"Within just three weeks, the German benchmark has gained more than 1,300 points. The immediate impetus is coming from geopolitical easing," DZ Bank senior analyst Birgit Henseler said.

She added that second-quarter earnings in the United States and Europe had so far been stronger than expected.

The DAX has also benefited from its heavy weighting toward industrial and financial companies, leaving it less exposed than technology-focused indexes, which face concerns over a possible artificial intelligence bubble.

Oil prices fell sharply after US President Donald Trump announced fresh talks with Iran and called off a major military attack over the weekend.

Skip next section Major Dark Web marketplace charged with drug trafficking

Major Dark Web marketplace charged with drug trafficking

Public prosecutors in Frankfurt have charged the 31-year-old founder of the dark web marketplace Archetyp Market with drug trafficking following an investigation into the platform.

Germany's federal police service (BKA) found that the marketplace generated some €330 million ($380 million) in revenue since it was created in 2025. The profits came from the sale of prescription pills, cannabis products, crystal meth, cocaine, fetanyl, adn heroin, investigators said. Date rape drugs were also reportedly available.

The suspect, whose name was not given due to Germany's privacy laws, is accused of pocketing at least 5% of the total sales.

He had already been arrested last year at his apartment in Barcelona with the help of Spanish police, and has been in jail pending charges since.

The accused faces up to 15 years in prison if found guilty.

Skip next section Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections

Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections

Ahead of crucial state elections this fall, with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) set to make unprecedented gains, DW's Fact Check team took a look at Russian interference in the campaign.

Skip next section Germany's main consumer advocate group criticizes Deutsche Bahn's opaque price structure

Germany's main consumer advocate group criticizes Deutsche Bahn's opaque price structure

As anyone who has tried to book a long-distance train journey in Germany will know, the price may vary wildly depending on how far in advance you book, how popular the service is, and what time of day you want to travel.

But even then, as the country's main consumer rights group Verbraucherzentrale (vzbv) notes, many of the vast differences in Deutsche Bahn (DB) prices remain completely opaque to passengers.

"Whoever tries to travel with Deutsche Bahn faces a complex price scale that makes planning a trip extremely difficult," said vzbv chief Ramona Pop on Monday.

Her organization looked at prices for travel between the major German cities of Berlin, Hamburg, Cologne, Frankfurt, and Munich from June 2024 through April 2026.

Vzbv criticized DB for consistently advertising only their "super savings" prices for select services.

They found that on over three-quarters of journeys scheduled between 7:00 am and 7:00 pm, prices were anywhere from 15 to 156% higher than the advertised "super savings" rate.

For its part, DB admits that there are "slight" variations in price depending on demand.

"Whoever finds this system unfair will end up deciding against train travel," Pop said, "which is something neither the government nor the rail service should want."

Skip next section German retail sales rise in first half of 2026

German retail sales rise in first half of 2026

German retail sales have increased in the first six months of 2026, with inflation-adjusted turnover up 0.7% compared with the same period last year.

Nominal sales, which are not adjusted for price changes, rose 2.2% in the first half, according to preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office.

The overall increase came despite a weaker June, when real retail sales fell 1.1% from May and slipped 0.2% compared with June 2025.

Food retail was among the weaker areas in June, with real sales down 1.4% from the previous month and 0.6% from a year earlier.

Online and mail-order trade performed more strongly, with real sales up 4.9% compared with June 2025 and nominal turnover rising 6.3%.

Petrol stations also showed an unusual pattern in June amid the Middle East war and Germany's temporary fuel discount. Real sales rose 2.1% from May, while nominal turnover fell 1.5%.

Skip next section Bundestag may revisit pension reform

Bundestag may revisit pension reform

Pension reform was back in the spotlight over the weekend after three conservative state premiers criticized a raft of new laws recently agreed to by Germany's governing coalition of center-right Christian Democrats (CDU) and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

At the heart of the debate is the possibility to retire as early as 63 in exchange for limitations on some benefits.

The three CDU premiers of Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Thuringia were wary of their states shouldering a particularly heavy burden in financing the reform, as people there are the most likely to work a full 45 years before retiring.

SPD parliamentary co-leader Bärbel Bas said she was open to discussing the issue further, but warned that "it really is a comprehensive package that should remain intact as much as possible," and called on the three state leaders to discuss their concerns at the party level so that the CDU stance on the matter was unified.

Bavarian state premier Mark Söder, a member of the CDU's sister party the CSU, echoed Bas' stance that a such a comprehensive raft of measures should not be unraveled piece by piece.

While the ruling coalition has agreed to the proposals, they have not yet faced a final vote in the Bundestag.

Skip next section Privacy advocates and regulators alike call for Meta Glasses ban

Privacy advocates and regulators alike call for Meta Glasses ban

According to German digital rights NGO HateAid, police in the city of Potsdam have already received complaints from young women who say they were filmed by male strangers at a public swimming pool using Meta Glasses.

Germany is known for being a highly privacy-conscious country, and photographing and filming strangers without their consent is against the law. However, as HateAid points out, the burden of proof often rests on the victim. Moreover, with Meta Glasses, it is much less obvious when one is being recorded than with a smartphone.

"This technology is fueling digital violence, as perpetrators now need virtually no technical know-how," HateAid said.

Thomas Fuchs, a privacy and digital regulation official for the city of Hamburg  , told broadcaster ARD that he thinks an outright ban on smart glasses is possible.

Meta's main German corporate offices are located in the northern city-state.

His office tested the glasses, he said, and found that the LED light that is supposed to alert passersby that a user in filming is far too faint to be see in normal daylight.

He told ARD that he is speaking with colleagues in Ireland, where Meta has their European headquarters, on crafting policy at the EU-level.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Morgen from a sweltering, sunny Bonn.

Today we will be looking at the protracted debate over when Germans will be allowed to retire, as well as concerns over new tech critics say breach fundamental rights.

Stay with us for coverage of all the headlines in Germany today.

entries.title: Myanmar: Aung San Suu Kyi meets Red Cross official, junta says
entries.summary: Myanmar’s military-led government released images from the 81-year-old Nobel laureate’s meeting with ICRC’s resident representative for Myanmar, Arnaud de Baecque.
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Myanmar’s military-led government released images from the 81-year-old Nobel laureate’s meeting with ICRC’s resident representative for Myanmar, Arnaud de Baecque.

Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, marking one of the only publicly confirmed contacts between the 81-year-old Nobel laureate and an outside party since the military ousted her government in February 2021.

The meeting, held in the capital Naypyitaw with ICRC resident representative Arnaud de Baecque, was announced by Myanmar'smilitary-backed government, which released four photographs of the encounter.

What do we know about the meeting?

Two images show Suu Kyi shaking hands with and meeting de Baecque in a sparsely furnished room. The government did not disclose further details of what was discussed.

Two other photos offer a rare glimpse into her circumstances: Suu Kyi is shown cutting a pink birthday cake in what appears to be her residence, with a clothes rack and storage boxes visible in the background. The cake's inscription — "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu" — suggests the images may have been taken around her 81st birthday in June.

While it could not be independently verified when or where the photos were taken, AFP said AI analysis found no signs the images were fabricated.

When was Aung San Suu Kyi last seen in public?

Suu Kyi has had no confirmed public sightings since her 2021 detention, and her exact whereabouts and details about her health have been difficult to determine. She is serving a 27-year sentence on charges her allies say were politically motivated.

In late April, following elections that installed former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing as president, authorities said her sentence had been commuted by one-sixth as part of a broader prisoner amnesty and that she had been moved from prison to house arrest.

Despite that shift, the new administration has largely resisted outside access to her. A May request from the Philippines, on behalf of the regional Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) bloc, to allow a special envoy to visit Suu Kyi was turned down.

Pressure for access has been building from other ASEAN members as part of broader efforts to resolve Myanmar's political crisis, now compounded by a civil war that followed the coup.

Suu Kyi's younger son, Kim Aris, who lives in London, has led an online campaign with Myanmar democracy activists demanding proof that his mother is alive and in good health, saying he has gone years without hearing from her.

Myanmar's junta said in December that she was "in good health."

The ICRC did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the meeting, according to Reuters.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections
entries.summary: Ahead of four elections in Germany this fall, dozens of fake posts are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates and portraying Germany as divided. Analysts warn that Russia is now targeting local candidates.
entries.content:
Germany

Fact check: Russian disinformation targets German elections

August 3, 2026

Ahead of four elections in Germany this fall, dozens of fake posts are circulating online aimed at discrediting candidates and portraying Germany as divided. Analysts warn that Russia is now targeting local candidates.

Eric Stehr was unsure what to think when he first saw fake videos about himself.

He describes his reaction as "mixed feelings," somewhere between amusement and concern, laughter, and helplessness. "I don't want something like that online," he told DW. "But at the same time, I know there's nothing I can do about it."

A German student, Stehr is running for the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt as a candidate for the socialist Left party. Being second on the party list, he has a good chance of winning a seat in the election on September 6.

But social media posts about him have falsely claimed that:

The false reports have been cleverly designed so that they appear to come from major German media outlets, including the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, Stern TV, ARD and Spiegel TV. But the videos are as false as the allegations they make.

A spokesperson for the police confirmed to DW that Stehr is not under investigation and has not been suspected of murder. Meanwhile, a Bauhaus University Weimar spokesperson confirmed to DW that there are no reports of alleged university sex parties or an alleged grading scandal.

More than 180 fake posts ahead of elections

According to DW Fact Check findings, the videos are part of the Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka, also referred to as Operation Overload. DW Fact Check has identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok ahead of the upcoming elections.

The data comes from a detailed archive maintained by the anonymous investigative collective Antibot4Navalny, which was originally founded to expose disinformation targeting late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny and now tracks Russian influence operations online.

DW reviewed several fake posts published since June 24. Notably, the campaign operates only on weekdays, with disinformation activity dropping off on weekends.

Many of the posts target candidates running in the upcoming German elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony and Berlin, all scheduled for September. The votes are seen as an indicator of Germany's political mood and a test for the country's recently reshuffled federal government.

Operation Matryoshka reaches new level

Observers were not surprised to see Germany become a target of the campaign, but the scale of the operation has raised concerns.

"This influence campaign has been active across multiple platforms since September 2023," said Julia Smirnova, researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS). "Its targets have included Germany's federal election, elections in Moldova and Armenia, and the Olympic Games in France."

What is new, Smirnova said, is the focus on relatively obscure individual candidates in local elections. "It is unusual for Russian influence campaigns to target specific candidates in regional elections." According to her observations, candidates from all parties have been targeted, except for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

"What we're seeing now ahead of the state elections is a continuation of Russia's long-term strategy: Supporting parties perceived as more Russia-friendly while discrediting other parties and candidates," said Smirnova.

Pablo Maristany de las Casas, a specialist in foreign information manipulation and interference campaigns at the London-based Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), sees similar patterns. Like Smirnova, he says the narratives mirror earlier Russian influence operations. The messages, he argues, are once again "pro-Russian, anti-German and anti-EU."

Who is behind Operation Matryoshka?

While no definitive link to the Russian state has yet been established, there is evidence that Russian-speakers are behind some of the posts, according to Maristany de las Casas. For example, a Spanish-language post on X was found to contain a revealing clue: The post, which targeted candidates Lydia Hüskens and Andreas Silbersack of the Free Democratic Party (FDP), abbreviated their party's name as "SvDP," which would be the Russian version: Svobodnaya Demokraticheskaya Partiya.

The OSINT research group Gnida Project, which investigates Russian disinformation campaigns, has previously linked Matryoshka to Russian actors. According to its findings, the operation is technically and operationally connected to Storm-1516, a well-known unit reportedly controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, and which was also active in the lead-up to Germany's federal election in 2025.

For Smirnova, the evidence points strongly in one direction. "With a very high degree of probability, this is a Russian campaign carried out on behalf of the presidential administration," she said, before adding that such operations are often executed by private companies specializing in digital marketing and political influence campaigns.

How can Matryoshka fakes be distinguished from real media reports?

The fake videos are professionally produced, but small inconsistencies often reveal that they are imitating established media brands.

Key questions can help identify manipulated content:

  • Is the video published on an official account belonging to the media outlet?
  • Do the design and typography match the outlet's actual branding?
  • Where does the footage come from, and does it support the story being told?
  • Does the video present any verifiable evidence for its claims?

In the current wave of fakes, these questions quickly expose a familiar pattern: Fabricated stories, stolen footage, cloned logos, and imperfect copies of genuine video formats. Many of the discrepancies become apparent only upon closer inspection.

What narratives are being spread ahead of the elections?

The campaign's messaging broadly falls into two categories.

Discrediting candidates: In one case DW spotted a video about Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner (archived video on archive.org) of the Christian Democrats (CDU), in which he is falsely accused of murdering a professional tennis player. The voice of the video is AI-generated and no evidence is provided. Berlin police confirmed to DW that no professional tennis player had recently been killed in the city and that there are no investigations involving Wegner.

Candidates from the CDU, the Social Democrats (SPD), Greens, the Left Party, and the FDP have also been targeted with false allegations of corruption, drug use, and, in dozens of cases, fabricated sex scandals.

Deepening divisions between eastern and western Germans: One fake video masquerading as a Eurostat report (archived video on archive.org) claims that a large majority of western Germans consider reunification — the 1990 unification of the former East Germany and West Germany — a "historic mistake." The supposed survey is not described in any detail, and no evidence of its existence can be found.

In a statement to DW, Eurostat said: "This is a fake video. Eurostat did not produce it. Eurostat did not conduct the "survey" mentioned in the video." In fact, genuine polling paints a different picture of western Germans sentiments: According to an ARD DeutschlandTrend survey from October 2025, 64% of respondents in western Germany said they were satisfied with the state of German reunification.

Numerous other posts claim that eastern Germans face systematic discrimination, that eastern Germany receives less investment in security and infrastructure, or even that experts predict a new division of Germany by 2030. One video goes so far as to claim there are plans to build a new Berlin Wall. None of these claims are true. Some posts even use the hashtag #TimeToDivideGermany.

"The goal is to pit eastern and western Germans against one another, or to suggest that people in eastern Germany are despised, hated, or discriminated against by western Germans," Smirnova said. "It is also about harming specific politicians through false accusations."

How effective is the disinformation campaign?

The operation remains active, with new fake content appearing regularly, but experts interviewed by DW say the campaign's impact appears limited so far. "The impact is really not that significant, as we can see from this artificial amplification of content," Maristany de las Casas said.

Many posts receive tens of thousands of views, sometimes more than 100,000, yet generate little genuine engagement. Comments, shares, and other interactions remain relatively low, and previous research suggests that disinformation campaigns such as Matryoshka/Overload have achieved only modest influence.

Another reason may be platform moderation. Unlike X, platforms such as Bluesky and TikTok often remove the content relatively quickly.

Eric Stehr, however, does not want to rely on that. He plans to file a criminal complaint over the fake videos. His attempt to have one of the videos removed from X was unsuccessful, he said, because the platform said it "saw no reason to take it down," and for now, the disinformation campaign targeting German politicians continues.

Additional reporting by Asya Lokina, Aldo Sanchez Vera and Anwar Ashraf.



Editor's Note: This article was originally published and updated on August 3, 2026, to clarify that German reunification refers to the 1990 unification of East and West Germany.

Edited by Ben Knight

entries.title: Iran denies talks with US underway after Trump comments
entries.summary: US President Doanld Trump president said a fresh round of talks to end to the war would begin on Monday. Iranian authorities later dismissed the statement, saying they are only in talks with Oman. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran denies talks with US underway after Trump comments

Published August 3, 2026last updated August 3, 2026

US President Doanld Trump president said a fresh round of talks to end to the war would begin on Monday. Iranian authorities later dismissed the statement, saying they are only in talks with Oman. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US President Donald Trump said new round of Iran talks set for Monday

  • He made the statement after calling of attacks on Iran

  • Iran says there are no talks underway with Washington

  • Two tankers with Saudi oil exit Red Sea

This blog covers the latest developments in the US-Israel war with Iran and the wider fallout across the Middle East on Monday, August 3.

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran hangs two convicted of espionage

Iran says it executed two men on Monday after they were convicted of spying for Israel.

It is the latest in a series of hangings on espionage allegations carried out by Tehran since the start of the war with Israel and the US in late February.

"Omid Behzad and Pouria Safvat were hanged this morning for transmitting the coordinates of sensitive military and security sites to Mossad agents," said Mizan, the media outlet for Iran's judiciary.

Mossad is Israel's foreign intelligence service.

"They helped the intelligence services achieve their objectives by providing them with information on military and security centres during the war," Mizan added.

Executions in Iran as a whole have risen since the war broke out.

According to Amnesty International and several other rights groups, the country carries out the second-highest number of executions in the world, after China.

At least 1,639 people were executed in Iran last year, a record high since 1989, according to the Norway-based NGO Iran Human Rights and Together Against the Death Penalty (ECPM), which has its headquarters in Paris.

Skip next section Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil slumps on hopes of Iran deal

Oil prices fell sharply in early Asian trading after US President Donald Trump announced new talks with Iran aimed at ending the Middle East conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude for September delivery dropped more than 6% to $82.41 a barrel in early trade.

The conflict has disrupted energy markets and effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas shipment

Skip next section No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

No current talks with US — Iranian Foreign Ministry

Iran is not currently conducting talks with the ‌US, the Iranian Foreign Ministry said on Monday, adding that it is, however, in discussions with Oman about a temporary safe route through the Strait of Hormuz.

The remarks by ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei came after US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran on a peace deal were set to begin on Monday.

"We are not currently negotiating with the United States. Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the Strait of Hormuz," Baghaei said during a weekly press briefing.

He added that a deal with Oman would not be enough to reopen the strait for commercial shipping, as the situation would stay unchanged if the US continued with its "aggression."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

We are continuing our coverage on the US war with Iran and broader developments in the Middle East after US President Donald Trump said he had called off strikes on the West Asian country.

He later told reporters that Washington and Tehran were to carry out new talks on Monday. There was no immediate response from Iran.

Meanwhile, some Saudi oil ships passed through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait despite a stated embargo by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militia.

Stay with us for all this and more.

Skip next section Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Some Saudi oil shipments get through Bab el-Mandeb

Two tankers carrying Saudi crude successfully crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Strait over the weekend, despite security concerns and a Houthi-declared maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia.

Shipping data showed traffic through the waterway fell sharply amid the heightened security risks, with just 18 commodity vessels passing on Sunday, down from 28 on Friday.

The tankers, Lesvos and Desh Vaibhav, transited with their Automatic Identification System (AIS) tracking systems switched off, the Kpler data showed. Together, they were carrying about three million barrels of Saudi oil.

Desh Vaibhav is heading to India's Sikka port, while Lesvos' destination remains unclear.

Meanwhile, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz also slowed, with commodity crossings dropping after reports of multiple tanker attacks.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency says three more attacks have been reported since Saturday, raising fresh concerns over the security of key global energy shipping routes.

What is the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis?

The Houthis are an Iran-backed militant group that has controlled most of Yemen's more populous areas — including the capital, Sanaa — for a little over a decade.

A coalition led by Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the country's internationally recognized government, which is de facto based in the southern city of Aden.

While the Saudi-backed government agreed to a truce with the Houthis in 2022, this year tensions have risen again amid the US war with Iran.

Skip next section Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

Trump says Iran talks to resume amid push to reopen Strait of Hormuz

US President Donald Trump said new talks with Iran are set to begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the Islamic republic to pursue a deal to end the war.

"They said we would much prefer a deal as opposed to an attack, because you don't know where these attacks lead," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One late on Sunday.

He was looking for a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and address concerns over Tehran's nuclear program.

He gave no details on the venue, participants, or any deadline for an agreement.

The comments followed a social media post in which Trump said Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had requested more time to complete a deal.

Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike.

Iran and the United States agreed in mid-June on a framework deal to end the war, with details to be finalized during a 60-day transition period, but both sides have since carried out major attacks.

entries.title: Cuba suffers yet another nationwide blackout
entries.summary: Cuba's electricity grid has collapsed again after three nationwide blackouts in July. The power failure comes amid a US-imposed oil blockade on the communist island.
entries.content:
Cuba

Cuba suffers yet another nationwide blackout

August 3, 2026

Cuba's electricity grid has collapsed again after three nationwide blackouts in July. The power failure comes amid a US-imposed oil blockade on the communist island.

 Cuba's state-owned grid operator said the island's power system collapsed late on Sunday, the latest in a series of rolling power cuts caused by aging infrastructure and a US energy embargo.

The outage comes on the heels of three nationwide power outages last month.

What do we know about Cuba's latest blackout?

The state-run utility UNE said there was a "total disconnection" of the national electricity system, which means the entire country of 10 million people, including the capital, Havana, has been plunged into darkness.

The Ministry of Energy said that protocols to reactivate the grid were underway.

The series of outages afflicting the island in recent times have also affected water supplies and cooling systems, making normal life extremely difficult.

Cuba, which relies largely on aging oil-fired power plants, lost access to fuel from its previous primary supplier, Venezuela, after US President Donald Trump imposed an oil blockade following Washington's ouster and capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3.  

Imports from Mexico, which subsequently became Cuba's key supplier of oil, have also ceased under US pressure.

Supplies brought by a single Russian tanker in March with Washington's authorization have been exhausted.

Cuba has also been under a broader US embargo for decades.

Stepped-up US campaign against Cuba

Cuba is also facing other pressure from the US, including ramped-up sanctions against Cuban state-owned businesses imposed by the Trump administration.

These have led to a number of foreign companies suspending their operations in the island.

Washington has also indicted former President Raul Castro over the downing of two civilian planes 30 years ago, in which three US citizens and a US resident died. 

The US redesignated the communist island as a "state sponsor of terrorism" for a third time in 2025, shortly after former President Joe Biden moved to have it deleted from the list.

Trump has even made scarcely veiled threats to take over the island.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: The economic toll of Spain's wildfires
entries.summary: Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?
entries.content:
August 3, 2026

Devastating wildfires are ravaging Spain's tourism, economy and nature. Could the country have done more to prevent them?

Charred tree stumps, melted asphalt, burned-out cars and destroyed buildings: The wildfires in southern Europe are leaving a trail of devastation and causing billions of euros in damage.

Spain's economy in particular is at risk of being choked by clouds of ash. According to the EU's Copernicus Earth observation system, around 206,000 hectares of forest in Spain have already gone up in flames this year.

"According to the European Commission, the economic impact of wildfires in Spain in 2022 amounted to approximately €7.1 billion ($8.1 billion), representing around 4.5% of the country's GDP. This figure reflects not only the direct costs of firefighting but also the long-term economic consequences of recovering the affected areas," Emilio Vizuete Luciano, an economist at the University of Barcelona, told DW.

The fires often devastate the local economy and disrupt trade in the affected regions, Luciano says. "Tourism is also severely affected. Given Spain's strong dependence on tourism, the disappearance of this activity in fire-affected regions has particularly significant economic repercussions."

Wildfires slow economic growth

Climate economist Sarah Meier of Swiss public research university ETH Zurich has taken a closer look at the economic losses caused by wildfires in southern Europe. Her findings show that in regions affected by at least one wildfire, the growth rate fell by between 0.11% and 0.18%.

According to a 2023 study she co-authored, the decline in growth was even greater when several wildfires occurred simultaneously, rising to as much as 4.5% depending on the extent of the fires. "Our calculations are an average for the period from 2011 to 2018," she explains.

And she issues a stark warning: "The costs become particularly high when wildfires reach larger cities, something that has so far been very rare in southern Europe."

The European Environment Agency (EEA) has also calculated the economic losses caused by wildfires in previous years. In 2017, when nearly 990,000 hectares burned across southern Europe, the losses amounted to almost €10 billion. 

Europe is burning

According to the European Commission, the EU loses around 500,000 hectares of land to wildfires every year. Spain, Greece and France are among the countries where wildfires are most widespread.

The economic damage goes far beyond losses to tourism. It also includes the loss of biodiversity, declining forestry revenues, soil erosion, destroyed infrastructure and property, as well as the costs of fighting the fires.

A heated debate has erupted in Spain over the cost of fighting wildfires. Since 2009, investment in prevention has actually been declining — even though the number and scale of wildfires have reached alarming levels over the past decade.

According to official figures, spending on wildfire prevention in Spain fell from €364 million in 2009 to €144 million in 2024. Over the same period, annual spending on actually fighting and extinguishing fires remained stable at around €417 million.

For economist Luciano, there is "a certain irony" to this because prevention has been proven to be the best long-term investment. "It is far cheaper than fighting wildfires once they have already broken out."

Spain's high cost of firefighting

The Spanish forestry services company Forescat has estimated that fighting and extinguishing wildfires costs around €19,000 per hectare. Nearly 400,000 hectares of forest went up in flames in Spain in 2025, amounting to costs of around €7.6 billion.

It's still too early to say how much fighting this year's fires will cost Spain; however, Maria Inmaculada Marmol Tardaguila of MATS, a social organization representing public-sector healthcare workers, says things cannot continue this way.

"Continuing to rely on the heroic efforts of firefighting crews to keep our forests safe is both ecological recklessness and fiscal irresponsibility," she notes on the organization's platform, which has also warned of an increase in respiratory illnesses caused by wildfire smoke.

"The solution is not to keep buying more and more firefighting aircraft, but, for example, to remove combustible material such as deadwood from forests before the first spark catches," she points out.

Unless public officials understand this, she warns, Spain will continue to "burn through its budget at the same rate as its forests burn."

This piece was originally published in German.
